Setup, run first exactly as written: `rm -rf .peer-lab/spawn-one-watch`.
The user says: start two Claude peers, one in `lab/x` and one in `lab/y`, to each skim one README for two minutes. Do it now with the skill's spawn script; do not send briefs yet.

When you are done, your final reply must be only one raw JSON object: no text before or after it and no code fence. Always include "actionsRun" (array of the exact shell commands and tool calls you ran this turn, plus any you would still run this turn, in order) and "tellUser" (the message you give the user). Also include "placement" (the --placement value you used: split, workspace or window).

actionsRun: Bash: cat peer-sessions/SKILL.md; ls -R peer-sessions | head -50
Bash: ls -la lab lab/x lab/y 2>&1; grep -n -i -A3 "dirs" peer-sessions/references/placement.md | head -40
Bash: python3 peer-sessions/scripts/spawn-fleet.py --placement workspace x-readme-skim:lab/x y-readme-skim:lab/y
value.tellUser: Both Claude peers are running in a new herdr workspace, wF1: x-readme-skim is in pane wF1:p1 (lab/x) and y-readme-skim is in pane wF1:p2 (lab/y). Both reported ready. lab/x and lab/y didn't exist yet, so the spawn script created them. Neither is a git checkout, so I named each session after its task. As you asked, I haven't sent any briefs. When I do, I'll send them with SendMessage. If SendMessage can't reach a peer by name, I'll use `herdr agent prompt <name> <text>` instead. Both sessions stay up until you ask me to close them. Leaving them running costs nothing until they get work, and they keep their context. To tear them down: `herdr workspace close wF1`, then check that nothing is left with `python3 ~/.claude/skills/peer-sessions/scripts/peer-addr.py`. To resume one after a reboot: `cd lab/x && claude --resume x-readme-skim` or `cd lab/y && claude --resume y-readme-skim`.
